doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Race, minstrelsy and taking jazz into the concert hall
summary: Why jazz became stigmatized: nineteenth-century lies, minstrelsy, and removing the music from social settings.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Is it because now it’s high art?

I think it’s — I don’t know. That’s possible. I think part of it is that, okay getting back to what we talked about quite a while ago, so the overwhelming headline in talking about anything about jazz and all this part of this conversation which we’re having, which is not biographical so much as about the state of jazz, you know there’s this looping headline all the time, which is race, okay? So let’s keep that in mind as it’s floating behind our heads while we’re talking. Okay. So what is it about jazz, how did this evolve? Well let’s look at it this way. There was a great, there was a great lie in the nineteenth century. And the lie is you’ve got to watch out for the male, for the black slave, because he’s going to escape and rape all the white women. Of course these prejudices are very much present in a lot of popular music today and in a lot of the racial hang-ups in our country in many ways. Now where does that come from? It comes from the fact that the truth is in the nineteenth century that the great amount of sexual shenanigans and crimes were committed by white slave owners against slaves, or enslaved people, depending on which term you prefer to use, okay. To cover up from the shame of that lie through minstrelsy and many, many other forms of popular entertainment, Americans to assuage that feeling of horrible guilt created the African-American male as a asexual cartoonish buffoonish kind of figure. All one has to do is watch Spike Lee’s film “Bamboozled” which we watch in my jazz history class sometimes, along with “Rashomon” but that’s another story. Okay. So to compensate for that feeling of guilt and that feeling of responsibility a certain type of minstrelsy evolves. Now eventually, white appropriation not withstanding, jazz evolves to the point where the French are taking it seriously and the European, other European countries are taking it intellectually and seriously, and America at some point, and boy I’m glossing over so much here, and culturally eventually says you know we should be proud of jazz. People all around the world say it’s so serious, we should be — and guess what we’re going to do? We’re going to take it out of its natural milieu, which would be like what John Batiste calls his band, Social Music, and what I think Louis Armstrong used terms like that, maybe even Ellington. Social music. It was somehow integrated with social functions, and not something abstract that one listens to like this, but, and so eventually what did we do? We killed it by putting it in the concert hall. Now © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

let me back up for a moment. I don’t mean we killed it by putting it in the concert hall, that’s a gloss. What I mean to say is that by taking it away from dancing and by taking it away from good times, what Albert Murray writes about in Stomping the Blues and many, many other places, there was a price to be paid. And the price that was paid that it found its place in the concert hall. Now you might ask yourself the question of why do people, especially in America, but why do we behave the way that we behave in the concert hall, listening to classical music? I mean it’s the strangest thing in the world, right? And I won’t go into — I have a long rap about this I do when I’m teaching and I’m sure you do too. But you know the behavior in the concert hall. The opening of the wrapper. The people who are asleep. The people that have no idea what the hell they’re listening to except they feel like they’re eating their spinach and they’re going to see a concert. And they don’t really — the great majority of them I don’t think are that engaged in it. Okay. Now we put jazz in there and take it away from its roots. I think the Ellington band probably had the healthiest diet of Carnegie Hall, colleges, great recordings, dances, dances, dances, dances, parties, parties. Great event. And so the music was informed by all these levels. That’s the beginning of kind of trying to come to terms with what we’re talking about. I’m sorry if I’m a little scattershot here because I’m merging, like you Monk, I’ve been teaching a long time and I have like, you know, these things that I do.
